aegisStory.text: Treat protection as work, not as a slogan. Drama comes from finite time, mass, power, fuel, pressure, medical capacity, docking geometry, route windows, escort coverage and human promises. The crew should solve problems through command judgment, navigation, engineering, rescue, logistics, medical care and restraint as often as through weapons.

rescueProcedural.text: Make cause and effect physically legible. Establish what is failing, who is endangered, what route or system can reach them, what resource the attempt consumes, and what new risk the choice creates. Rescue action should feel procedural, tactile and specific rather than miraculous.

civilianScale.text: Civilians are people with jobs, families, cargo, obligations, fear, competence and conflicting priorities, not anonymous disaster scenery. Large evacuations still need individual human anchors and practical details such as bags, medication, food, manifests, tools, children, elders, pets, cargo and mobility limits when relevant.

aegisVigilIdentity.text: The vessel is RFV Aegis Vigil, an Aegis-line Rex Fleet heavy cruiser. Never call the vessel Aegis Crown. Aegis Crown is the political and philosophical Crown tradition only. Aegis Vigil should read as a large working protection vessel: scarred, maintained, dependable, heavily redundant and built to remain useful while taking damage.

combatRestraint.text: When combat occurs, stage it around the protected objective. Aegis Vigil does not seek spectacle or destruction for its own sake; weapons, maneuver and armor are used to buy time, open a route, absorb pressure, screen civilians or end a threat. Do not default every crisis into a battle.
